title: Hurricane Maria
description:
Interview (A) with Maj. Gen. Thomas J. Sharpy, Deputy Commanding General for Lt. Gen. Buchanan, at Muniz Air National Guard Base, Puerto Rico, Oct. 12, 2017.
Hurricane Maria formed in the Atlantic Ocean and affected islands in the Caribbean Sea, including Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. U.S. Military assets supported FEMA as well as state and local authorities in rescue and relief efforts. (U.S. Air Force video by Senior Airman Tayor Harrison)
keywords: ANG, relief efforts, Puerto, Hurricane Maria, Rico Air National Guard, NGB, Puerto Rico

transcript.text: I'm the Deputy Commanding General for Lieutenant General Buchanan and since I've arrived I've
primarily been focusing on setting up the strategic airlift bridge that's been necessary to bring
the equipment, the personnel and all the supplies here to the island of Puerto Rico.
So the role of the Air Force obviously it's an island destination and due to the destruction
that this island suffered the airports and the seaports were closed.
So as soon as the winds were within limits the contingency response forces of the United
States Air Force came in and opened up the airfield in San Juan.
Once they opened the airfield they then opened up the cargo yard so that we could bring in
the much needed supplies forces into this airfield and then once we opened San Juan we
then went to Roosevelt Roads which is on the eastern side of the island and once we opened
up that airfield and cargo handling facility we then looked to the western side of the
island and Agua Día where we had to do the same thing and then the last airfield we opened
was Ponce which is in the southern central part of the island and then beyond the airfields
we then are also evaluating the seaports we know the one in San Juan is operating but we're
trying to get another one opened in Ponce so that we can bring in the large container vessels
that bring in the majority of supplies whether it be on a daily basis that the people of
Puerto Rico need and also to sustain a large military presence that's here.
Well obviously being an island destination everything you can't drive it in by a truck
everything has to be delivered by either air or by sea and initially the seaports were
closed and so therefore all of the cargo all the personnel and all the supplies had
to be airlifted in and we've flown almost 1400 sorties just in support of our fellow citizens
here in Puerto Rico.
It's been pretty awesome you know the Lieutenant General Birkanen brought his staff here from
Army North and they are fine oiled machine you know they were in Texas dealing with Harvey
and then they were in Florida dealing with Irma and then they came here to deal with
Maria and they have a lot of experience doing this.
The challenge for me was trying to integrate the strategic airlift because in those other
instances they had a lot of ground movement and a lot of forces that they had that were
quickly able to respond whereas here we had to fly everything in and so that strategic
airlift piece was that critical lifeline between our North and North Com and support a FEMA
that was run out of Florida by first Air Force and so I was there just to integrate and make
sure that we met the priorities of not only the Governor FEMA but also General Buchanan
in his role as the Joint Forces Land Component Commander.
I would say the biggest challenge has been we have a lot of great people trying to do
a lot of incredible things we all realize the magnitude of trying to provide relief
and those critical supplies and medical capabilities to our fellow citizens.
The challenge has been to integrate all of those efforts into a cohesive plan.
FEMA has a way of doing things the Army has a way of doing things the Air Force has a
way of doing things North Com has a way of doing things and just trying to coordinate
all those great efforts into a synchronized plan has been a challenge but I will tell you
I think we have done exceptionally well and I think the results that I have seen at all
the places that I have gotten to visit we are getting the commodities to the logistical
staging areas and we are using the municipalities and the mayors to distribute those goods to
getting them to the people that are in need.
It is going well could it be better absolutely but every day I have seen an improvement in
the teamwork has just been incredible.
I think the biggest success has been that this is in my 30 years in the Air Force I have
never seen us provide this much weight of effort for humanitarian assistance as a release
effort whether it be an aircraft, whether it be personnel or whether it be in the amount
of DOD effort that we have put behind this.
We have moved over 1,300 sorties just for Maria alone here in Puerto Rico and over 2,000
within the US Virgin Islands in the Puerto Rican area of responsibility in the last 40 days.
That is incredible.
I have got to tell you everywhere I have been including today when I was in Roosevelt Roads
I saw an airman who was on the flight line.
He was tired, he was dirty, he was thirsty and he was drenched in sweat but you know what
I have never seen Morale higher.
You know why?
Because he was doing what he wanted to do and he was doing it for a cause that is bigger
than himself because he knows that at the end of the day his efforts enable the relief
supplies to get to those families, to get to those children and without everyone who is
here we wouldn't be able to do what we are doing because we are making a difference.
I have seen it in the field, I have seen it when I delivered cargo to the isolated communities
in the mountains yesterday.
First of all the people of Puerto Ricans, they are dedicated, resilient, passionate
and as they have told me this is a storm.
It is not going to get in the way of them being a proud people that they are.
Specifically you know we talk about the Air National Guard and the Reserve members that
are here in Puerto Rico.
Not only did they serve our country but they are also victims in this as well.
And so they are not only proud of their service but they are also struggling with the devastation
that them and their families have found.
And I will tell you they are the first ones to raise their hands because they want to support
their families and their fellow members in Puerto Rico.
Now what I found even more inspiring to me was how many people who are from Puerto Rico
who serve in our Department of Defense around the nation and around the world who volunteered
to be some of the first ones here to be able to be the translators, to be able to be the
facilitators because they are going back to their neighborhoods.
I talked to a Warren officer yesterday who had the ability to go back to a neighborhood
and the people were looking at him kind of puzzled and then they told him his name.
They all said you are the little guy that used to cause trouble in the neighborhood and
they broke down and let him go because it was his neighborhood, it was his family that
he was providing support to.
And I have never seen a soldier more proud of what he is doing because he is helping a
neighborhood we grow up.
We say that the great news about our garden reserve is you live locally, serve globally
when you get to live locally and serve locally that is a huge success and the fact that they
are leading a lot of the efforts matters because they believe that it is their neighborhood,
it is their families that they are helping and we are here to help support them as well.
It is pretty cool.
Is there anything else you would like to add?
I just like to add that when I first got here and I got to see the devastation my heart
sunk.
You know what I saw in the press before I left Scott Air Force Base and got an airplane
to come here, I knew that it was bad but when I saw the devastation firsthand first by flying
around the country, second by driving to some of the locations my heart sank.
And the good news is the people are resilient.
I was blown away by how supportive they were, how happy they were and how they were really
ready to get on to get back to normal and get on with their lives.
Our goal is to get that to happen sooner rather than later and that is why we have had so many
incredible support from the Department of Defense.
In fact when the President said you have everything you need I looked him in the eye and said
yes we do because we are not shying away from this one and we are not going to leave until
the normal is back here in Puerto Rico.
